title: Contains Duplicate: check using HashSet in O(n).
shortTitle: Contains Duplicate: Check Using a HashSet in O(n)
keyPoints: Add each element to a HashSet; the first time add() returns false, you have found a duplicate.
Average O(n) time because each HashSet add and contains is O(1) average, with O(n) extra space for the set.
Early exit on the first duplicate avoids scanning the rest of the array.
Pre-sizing the HashSet to expected capacity avoids internal rehashing.
Sorting first and scanning adjacent elements is O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space if mutation is allowed.
For BigDecimal, equals considers scale, so normalise with stripTrailingZeros() before adding to the set.

s1_definition.oneliner: Add each element to a HashSet; the first time add returns false you have a duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Contains Duplicate** – a problem that asks whether any value appears more than once in a collection.
- **HashSet approach** – scan the collection once, calling `add()` for each element; `add()` returns `false` when the element already exists, signalling a duplicate.
- **Time complexity** – average O(n) because each `add()` is O(1) average, one per element.
- **Space complexity** – O(n) for the set, the classic time-for-space trade-off.
- **Alternative** – sort first, then scan adjacent elements for O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space if mutation is allowed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction identifiers and must be sure none was submitted twice, because a duplicate identifier means a transaction could be applied twice and Rajesh could be charged twice. A clerk keeps a box of identifiers already seen and drops each new identifier in. The moment an identifier is already in the box, the clerk shouts "duplicate" and stops. Checking the box is near-instant, so the whole batch is cleared in one quick pass.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Input: ["TXN-001", "TXN-002", "TXN-003", "TXN-001"]

  Step 1: seen = {}
          add("TXN-001") --> true  (newly added)
          seen = {TXN-001}

  Step 2: add("TXN-002") --> true  (newly added)
          seen = {TXN-001, TXN-002}

  Step 3: add("TXN-003") --> true  (newly added)
          seen = {TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003}

  Step 4: add("TXN-001") --> false (already present)
          DUPLICATE FOUND --> return true

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HashSet.add(element)             │
  │  ┌─────────┐    ┌───────────┐    │
  │  │ hash(e) │--->│ bucket[i] │    │
  │  └─────────┘    └─────┬─────┘    │
  │                       │          │
  │               already present?   │
  │              /         \         │
  │           YES           NO       │
  │         return         add to    │
  │         false          bucket    │
  │                       return     │
  │                        true      │
  └───────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once, and the fast solution is a single pass with a HashSet. I add each element to the set, and because `add()` returns false when the element is already present, the first time it returns false I have found a duplicate and return true immediately. If every add succeeds, there are no duplicates. It is average O(n) time with O(n) space for the set.

The trade-off is memory for speed. The HashSet approach is the fastest average-case option, but if memory is tight and I may mutate the input, sorting first and scanning adjacent elements finds duplicates in O(n log n) with no extra space. The brute-force double loop is O(n squared) and only acceptable for tiny inputs. I choose the approach based on the constraints.

The correctness point I always stress is equality and hashing. HashSet depends on `equals()` and `hashCode()` being consistent, so for custom key types I override both. For BigDecimal there is a famous trap: `equals()` considers scale, so `100` and `100.00` are not equal and hash differently. When numeric equality is what matters, I normalise the scale with `stripTrailingZeros()` before adding to the set.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this to guard a batch of transaction identifiers before applying them, because a repeated identifier could double-charge a customer like Rajesh. The guard pre-sizes the set, exits at the first duplicate, and for monetary amounts normalises scale so numerically equal values are caught.

Remember one sentence: add each element to a HashSet and check the return value of `add()` – false means duplicate found, in O(n) time.
